title: Adobe Engineering Director Moves Back to Bengaluru After a Decade in the US
excerpt: The senior executive's decision to relocate for family adds to a growing wave of reverse migration among Indian tech professionals in Silicon Valley.
body:
• An Adobe director of engineering has relocated from the Bay Area to Bengaluru after 10 years in the United States, citing the desire to be closer to family.
  • The executive acknowledged missing the Bay Area but said family proximity ultimately outweighed career considerations in the US.
  • The move reflects a broader reverse migration trend among senior Indian tech professionals, accelerated by remote work flexibility, H-1B uncertainty, and India's growing tech ecosystem.

An Adobe director of engineering has moved back to Bengaluru after spending a decade in the United States, joining a growing cohort of senior Indian tech professionals choosing to return home for personal and family reasons.

The executive, who held a senior engineering leadership role at Adobe's operations in the Bay Area, said the decision was driven primarily by a desire "to be closer to family." In social media posts that went viral over the weekend, the director acknowledged the trade-offs involved, noting "we miss the Bay Area" while emphasizing that proximity to aging parents and extended family in India ultimately tipped the balance.

Part of a Broader Wave

The move is the latest high-profile example of what researchers and migration experts have dubbed "reverse brain drain" — the return of experienced Indian professionals from the United States and other Western countries to India. While the phenomenon is not new, it has gained momentum in recent years, driven by a confluence of factors.

Remote work arrangements normalized during the pandemic have made it feasible for some professionals to maintain US-level roles while living in India. At the same time, increased uncertainty around H-1B visa renewals and green card backlogs — which can stretch decades for Indian-born applicants — has prompted many to reconsider the long-term calculus of staying in the US.

"At some point, you have to choose between the life that looks good and the life that feels right."

— A tech professional who recently returned to India from the US

India's Tech Pull Factor

India's technology sector has also become a more compelling destination for senior talent. Bengaluru, which hosts global R&D centers for companies including Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and Adobe itself, now offers roles that rival Silicon Valley in technical complexity if not always in compensation. Adobe's Bengaluru operations are among the company's largest outside the US, covering products from Creative Cloud to the AI-powered Adobe Learning Manager platform.

Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has been among the most vocal advocates for Indian tech professionals to return, arguing that "Bharat Mata needs your talent" and that India's path to global influence runs through technological self-sufficiency. His appeals have resonated particularly as political dynamics in the US have shifted, with some Indian professionals reporting a less welcoming environment.

The Compensation Trade-Off

The financial calculus of returning remains complex. While base salaries in India's tech sector have risen sharply — director-level engineering roles at top firms in Bengaluru now command ₹80 lakh to ₹1.5 crore annually — they still lag US equivalents, where total compensation at the same level can exceed $400,000. However, lower costs of living, domestic help availability, and proximity to family networks often offset the nominal pay gap for those who have accumulated US savings.

For Adobe specifically, the timing aligns with a leadership transition at the company. CEO Shantanu Narayen, himself an Indian-origin executive who rose through Adobe's ranks after emigrating from Hyderabad, announced in March 2026 that he would step down after 18 years, with a successor search underway.

What It Means for NRIs

The Adobe director's move underscores a shifting narrative around the Indian American professional trajectory. Where the one-way journey from IIT to Silicon Valley was once the default aspiration, an increasing number of established professionals are plotting return paths — bringing with them management expertise, global networks, and technical depth that strengthens India's innovation ecosystem.

For NRIs weighing similar decisions, the key variables remain unchanged: family considerations, career trajectory, financial planning around RNOR tax status and asset repatriation, and children's education. But the social stigma that once attached to "going back" has diminished considerably, replaced by a recognition that the choice is less about retreat and more about recalibration.
